look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST — TEXAS CROTON / SKUNKWEED: an annual with relatively narrow, alternate, entire-edged leaves, pale stellate hairs and often open branching. DO NOT identify it from silver-gray foliage or white flower clusters alone. This species is DIOECIOUS: an individual plant bears either staminate (MALE) flowers or pistillate (FEMALE) flowers. Male flowers expose many pale stamens. Confirm female plants by a distinctly WARTY / verrucose, three-part capsule; seek actual fruit macros. The installed Joey photographs are of a MALE specimen and cannot demonstrate female fruit or, by themselves, prove that the species has separate-sex plants. Contrast the woody, minutely serrulate C. fruticulosus and the smaller low-branching monoecious C. monanthogynus / C. lindheimerianus.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Texas croton is a dioecious ANNUAL with relatively narrow, entire leaves and a wart-covered female capsule. Shrubby C. fruticulosus has persistent WOODY stems and finely serrulate leaves. Prairie tea C. monanthogynus and three-seed C. lindheimerianus are monoecious, smaller and often low branching; female fruit/style evidence is more decisive than leaf fuzz alone.

not_reliable_alone: Narrow leaves: male and female plants of Texas croton can differ in leaf width and overlap other species.
White flower clusters: male stamens show male reproductive structures, not evidence for dioecy on one photographed individual.
Pale stellate hairs: a genus-level character, not an exact species confirmation.
A smooth immature female ovary should not be mislabeled as mature warty fruit; inspect mature capsule surface.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.title: Texas croton: male stamens now; female warted fruit next

steps.look: Openly branched annual with alternate narrow simple leaves
steps.what: Use the recorded full-plant image to learn the overall appearance. This clue is not sufficient by itself.

steps.look: Many pale projecting stamens in open, small flowers
steps.what: The installed Joey Santore macro shows actual staminate flowers and hairy stems. Male stamens are NOT female style branches.

steps.look: Separate pistillate flower clusters, without conspicuous male stamens
steps.what: This species is dioecious; check a DIFFERENT flowering individual and photograph the whole female cluster with a millimeter scale. Existing gallery is male-only.
Take a sharp side-on and top-down macro showing actual raised bumps on the fruit and its three lobes. This is the leading missing decisive photo.

steps.look: Persistent woody base, tiny serrations of leaf edge
steps.what: For C. fruticulosus, photograph woody crown and finely toothed margin; a leafy branch alone does not show the habit difference.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: TEXAS CROTON = NARROW ANNUAL + SEPARATE SEXES + WARTY FEMALE CAPSULE. Current photos show its MALE side only.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Croton texensis: male-flower learning card / female capsule still missing
steps: Observe a branched annual with alternate, narrow and generally entire leaves.
In the existing Joey photo, notice projecting MALE stamens; do not call these female styles.
Locate another reproductive plant: true pistillate material should lack stamens because this species is dioecious.
On a mature female capsule, document actual raised WARTS and a three-lobed outline. Female photo not in this gallery.
If woody base or tiny leaf-edge teeth are present, compare C. fruticulosus before settling on the ID.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Annual + dioecious + female warty capsule. Male-only field ID is tentative without independent supporting characters.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Existing photographic evidence is male-only. Dioecy and the distinctive female mature capsule are referenced from botanical treatments, not demonstrated by installed images.
